extracted.intended_audience: cosmetic manufacturers, packers, distributors, importers, and regulatory compliance personnel
extracted.subtask_description: Compliance and product-safety requirements from 21 CFR Part 700 governing cosmetics: definitions, prohibited ingredients/practices, packaging/labeling rules, recordkeeping, and import/country-designation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions (terms used in subchapter)
rubrics_metrics.description: As used in this subchapter: definitions of act, cosmetic product, flavor, fragrance, ingredient, proprietary ingredient, chemical description, cosmetic raw material, commercial distribution, establishment, manufacture, packaging, all business trading names used by the establishment, system of commercial distribution, filed screening procedure, reportable experience, and applicability of definitions in sections 201, 601, and 602 of the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes precise statutory and regulatory meanings such as: 'cosmetic product' means a finished cosmetic; 'commercial distribution' means annual gross sales in excess of $1,000; 'chemical description' means a concise definition using standard chemical nomenclature or, when not possible, source and processing. 'Filed screening procedure' must be on file with FDA, designed to determine reasonable basis that alleged injury did not occur with use, and be audit-able. 'Reportable experience' defined with examples and exclusions (e.g., those determined unfounded by a filed screening procedure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosmetics containing bithionol (adulteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any cosmetic containing bithionol is deemed to be adulterated under section 601(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FDA view: bithionol is deleterious due to photosensitivity and cross-sensitization risks; regulatory proceedings may be initiated for products shipped after March 15, 1968.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mercury compounds (restrictions and exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercury-containing cosmetic preparations used as skin-bleaching agents are regarded as drugs and cosmetics and are generally misbranded and/or adulterated; mercury in cosmetics is disfavored because of toxicity, accumulation, allergenicity, and availability of less toxic substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FDA withdraws prior permissive opinions. Any product containing mercury as a skin-bleaching agent offered for sale as such is misbranded and may be a new drug without approval; subject to regulatory action if shipped after Jan 5, 1973. Cosmetics containing mercury are adulterated unless they meet either: (i) contain no more than a trace amount unavoidable under GMP and less than 1 part per million (0.0001 percent) calculated as metal; or (ii) intended for use only in the eye area, contain no more than 65 ppm (0.0065 percent) mercury as preservative, and no effective/safe nonmercurial preservative is available for such cosmetics. Agency rationale and exceptions (eye-area) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vinyl chloride in aerosol cosmetic products (prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any cosmetic aerosol product containing vinyl chloride as an ingredient is deemed to be adulterated under section 601(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: inhalation exposure in confined spaces may exceed safe occupational levels; vinyl chloride linked to acute toxicity and carcinogenic effects; subject to regulatory action for products shipped within the Act's jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of certain halogenated salicylanilides (prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Halogenated salicylanilides (tribromsalan, dibromsalan, metabromsalan, and 3,3′,4,5′-tetrachlorosalicylanilide) are deleterious substances and any cosmetic containing them at any level is deemed adulterated under section 601(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: potent photosensitizers and cross-sensitizers causing disabling skin disorders; safer alternatives available. Products introduced into interstate commerce after Dec 1, 1975 not in compliance are subject to regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of zirconium in aerosol cosmetic products (prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any aerosol cosmetic product containing zirconium is deemed to be adulterated under section 601(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: certain zirconium compounds have caused skin granulomas and toxic effects in lungs and other organs; aerosol use can deliver zirconium to deep lung tissue. Products introduced after Sept 15, 1977 not in compliance are subject to regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of chloroform as an ingredient (prohibition with limited residual exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any cosmetic product containing chloroform as an ingredient is adulterated and subject to regulatory action under sections 301 and 601(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: chloroform associated with carcinogenic effects in animals and absorbed via skin, respiratory, and GI systems. Exception: residual chloroform from use as a processing solvent during manufacture, or as a byproduct from synthesis of an ingredient, is not considered to be 'chloroform as an ingredient' for the purpose of this section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of methylene chloride as an ingredient (prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any cosmetic product that contains methylene chloride as an ingredient is deemed adulterated and is subject to regulatory action under sections 301 and 601(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: long-term animal inhalation studies show increased tumors and FDA concluded cosmetic use poses significant cancer risk to consumers (notably in aerosol hair sprays where concentrations ranged 10–25%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) propellants (prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of chlorofluorocarbons in cosmetics as propellants in self-pressurized containers is prohibited as provided in § 2.125 of this chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short directive referencing cross-cited prohibition in chapter/section §2.125.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tamper-resistant packaging requirements (scope, design, labeling, exemptions, effective dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers/packers packaging cosmetic liquid oral hygiene products or products used vaginally for retail sale must package them in a tamper-resistant package if accessible to the public while held for sale; noncompliance may render the product adulterated or misbranded under sections 601/602.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope: mainly cosmetic liquid oral hygiene and vaginal products. Tamper-resistant package definition: an indicator or barrier to entry which, if breached or missing, can reasonably be expected to provide visible evidence of tampering; indicator/barrier must be distinctive by design or use an identifying characteristic (pattern, name, trademark, logo, picture). Tamper-resistant features may involve immediate-container/closure or secondary-container/carton systems; must remain intact under reasonable handling. Labeling: retail packages (except aerosol products) must bear a prominent statement alerting consumers to the specific tamper-resistant feature; statement must be placed so it is unaffected if the feature is breached or missing; if identifying characteristic used, it must be referenced in labeling. Exemptions: manufacturer/packer may request exemption via a citizen petition under §10.30 with specific elements (product name, reasons compliance is unnecessary or cannot be achieved, description of alternative steps taken or available, other justification). Effective dates for packaging/labeling phased (various dates in 1983–1984) and specific effective-date notes and stays are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prohibited cattle materials — definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines 'prohibited cattle materials' (specified risk materials, small intestine of all cattle except as provided, material from nonambulatory disabled cattle, material from cattle not inspected and passed, or mechanically separated (MS) beef) and related terms including 'inspected and passed', 'mechanically separated (MS) (Beef)', 'nonambulatory disabled cattle', 'specified risk material', 'tallow', 'tallow derivative', and 'gelatin'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed definitions include measurement/processing standards (e.g., tallow insoluble impurity limit 0.15% determined by AOCS Official Method Ca 3a-46 or equivalent), specific anatomical definitions for specified risk material (brain, skull, eyes, spinal cord, vertebral column and other named tissues), and references to incorporated methods and locations for consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prohibited cattle materials — requirements, recordkeeping, importer obligations, and adulteration
rubrics_metrics.description: No cosmetic shall be manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contain prohibited cattle materials; small intestine may be excepted if distal ileum removed by specified procedure; failure to comply renders a cosmetic adulterated under section 601(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small intestine exception requires removal of at least 80 inches of uncoiled and trimmed small intestine from caeco-colic junction proximally, or an establishment-demonstrated equally effective procedure. Records: manufacturers/processors must establish and maintain records sufficient to demonstrate nonuse of prohibited cattle materials, retain records for 2 years, keep records at the establishment or reasonably accessible location, electronic records acceptable if onsite-accessible, and records must be available to FDA for inspection and copying. Importers: when filing customs entry, importer of record must affirm whether cosmetic was manufactured from/processed with/or contains cattle material and affirm manufacture in accordance with this section; if cosmetic contains cattle material, importer must provide, if requested, within 5 days records sufficient to demonstrate compliance. Records that meet §11.3(b)(6) definition of electronic records are exempt from part 11, but records also required under other statutes/regulations remain subject to part 11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process for designating countries (prohibited-cattle-materials exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A country may request designation by FDA to allow certain cattle materials to be considered inspected/passed and not 'prohibited cattle materials'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request must be written to the Director, Office of the Center Director, CFSAN, include BSE case history, risk factors, measures to prevent BSE introduction/transmission, and other relevant info. FDA will respond in writing, may impose conditions, and any designation is subject to future review and possible revocation if no longer appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosmetics containing sunscreen ingredients — drug-regulation trigger and labeling qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: A product that uses the term 'sunscreen' or similar sun protection terminology in labeling or otherwise represents it prevents, cures, treats, or mitigates disease or affects body structure/function is a drug under section 201(g)(1); such use generally causes the product to be subject to regulation as a drug. If sunscreen ingredients are used for nontherapeutic/nonphysiologic purposes, to avoid consumer misunderstanding the term 'sunscreen' must be qualified by describing the cosmetic benefit provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The qualifying information must appear prominently and conspicuously at least once in the labeling in conjunction with the term 'sunscreen' or similar terminology. Example: 'Contains a sunscreen—to protect product color.' Clarifies that sunscreen active ingredients affect structure/function by absorbing/reflecting/scattering solar radiation and may prevent sunburn; labeling expectations are to avoid implying drug effects if not intended as a drug.
